data_flow: Raw $_POST['value'] is only passed through stripslashes() and written with file_put_contents() to uploads/booking-package/front_end.js (line 6066) without sanitisation. That file is enqueued and served to every front-end visitor (index.php:1175, 3970), so script injected here runs on all pages.

$_POST['key'] goes through sanitize_text_field() only (index.php:4568 to Setting.php:2831) and is used as the wp_options name in update_option($key, $token) at line 2841. A non-admin editor can therefore overwrite arbitrary site options (for example siteurl or active_plugins) with a hash value.

The per-booking cancellationToken is hash('ripemd160', timeKey . scheduleUnixTime . microtime(true)), built only from public slot values and a microsecond clock reading, not from a CSPRNG. Anyone who can narrow the booking time can guess it and then retrieve full booking details (myBookingDetails) or cancel the booking via key plus token.

The capability check computes $download, but when it is false and DOING_AJAX is true, the code skips wp_die and falls through to a nonce-only check on $_POST['nonce'] for the action 'package_app_action_download'. That nonce is generated with wp_create_nonce() and printed as 'nonce_download' into the front-end booking page, so anonymous visitors can obtain a valid value. The request then calls booking_package_schedule::getDownloadCSV() (lib/Schedule.php:7260), which takes $_POST['accountKey'] and date fields and returns booked-customer rows, including guest data, as a CSV attachment.

The handler takes $_POST['customer_id_for_subscriptions'] and $_POST['subscriptions_id_for_subscriptions'] (sanitize_text_field only) and passes them to Setting::lookingForSubscription() (lib/Setting.php:6281). That method performs a remote request, then calls updateSubscribeSite() and writes subscription and license option values from the response. No capability check and no nonce are applied, so any visitor can trigger license/subscription state changes for the site.

In selectedMode(), the 'refreshToken' branch passes the raw $_POST['key'] to Setting::refreshToken(). The method only applies sanitize_text_field() and then calls update_option($key, $token), so the caller chooses the name of any WordPress option to overwrite. The guard is only the Editor-level check (edit_others_posts or the plugin's editor/manager roles) in selectedMode(), with no allowlist on option names. The written value is a hash, so the attacker controls the option name rather than the value.

Unauthenticated POST customer_id_for_subscriptions and subscriptions_id_for_subscriptions (sanitize_text_field only, no nonce or capability check) -> Setting::lookingForSubscription (lib/Setting.php:6281-6370) sends them to the vendor API, then writes the returned subscription fields to plugin options and sets the subscription status to Active.

Editor-level POST value -> stripslashes -> file_put_contents to the uploads directory as front_end.css / front_end.js with no sanitisation, and that file is loaded on public pages, so script content can be stored for every visitor. Gated by edit_others_posts or the plugin's manager/editor roles, not by a manage_options check.

A rating field value from the anonymous submission is stored unsanitized in submit meta (no server-side type validation for rating in setup_from_post_section). When the value is non-numeric or outside 0..rating_max, the rating branch assigns the raw value to $value (line 405) and returns it without esc_html, so the markup reaches the admin list HTML.

The 'orderby' request parameter is passed through sanitize_text_field (which does not escape quotes or parentheses) and, when it has no numeric field prefix so absint() yields 0, it is returned verbatim at line 2017. The result is concatenated into the ORDER BY clause in db_read_all() (class-ws-form-submit.php:400) without prepare or whitelisting. Access requires read_submission, which the administrator role holds.

The 'orderby' request query var is read by WS_Form_Common::get_query_var in get_search_order_by, passed to get_order_by, and only run through sanitize_text_field and strtolower. If the value is not one of the whitelisted column names and contains no digits after removing the field prefix, the raw string is returned unescaped and concatenated into the ORDER BY clause of the SQL built in db_read_all (class-ws-form-submit.php:400).

WS_Form_Common::option_get('license_key') (api/class-ws-form-api-helper.php:576 calls get_license_key_obscured) returns the stored license key's last six characters, which are included in the response of an unauthenticated REST route; the route's permission callback is `return true` and no capability check is made.

Shortcode attributes such as file, attachments, data_file, page_watermark and client_certificate are not whitelisted in eval_shortcode (lines 940-958), so they are stored in the button's encrypted options blob. save_as_pdf_pdfcrowd decrypts that blob and merges it into options (1636-1647), prepare_conv routes these keys into the files list (1266-1268, 1278), and build_body passes the unvalidated path to file_get_contents (1107) and uploads the file contents to the converter, returning the resulting PDF to the requester.

Shortcode attributes button_custom_indicator, button_indicator_timeout and email_custom_dialogs are copied into the $config array (611-626, 577-578, 699) and JSON-encoded with json_encode, which does not escape single quotes. The JSON is then concatenated unescaped into a single-quoted onclick attribute at line 713, so the value can break out of the attribute and inject event-handler markup into the stored post output.

The url shortcode attribute is stored in the encrypted options blob and read in do_post_request (1182, 1191), which calls get_url, which calls wp_remote_get on it (993) with no host or IP restriction (not wp_safe_remote_get). The fetched body is then embedded in the PDF or the error page returned to the visitor.

The location POST value is accepted as the URL when its host matches the permalink host (1456-1484) and is assigned to options['url']. When the fetch returns an HTTP status of 400 or higher, get_url embeds $url unescaped in an href and in the link text (1018), and the message is echoed as HTML by save_as_pdf_pdfcrowd (1742, 1784).

The sanitization branch for button_indicator_html writes wp_kses_post output into $attrs['button_custom_html'] instead of $attrs['button_indicator_html'] (line 931), so the raw button_indicator_html value is kept. It is then appended unescaped to the button markup (736-737) and rendered in the post content.

The file name from get_output_name (1061-1086, which rawurldecodes the URL segment or uses output_name directly) is concatenated into $tmp_dir without sanitization (1517), and fopen with mode x creates the file at the resulting path (1518). The file is removed after the mail attempt, so the write is transient.

When the post author lacks unfiltered_html, the code should wp_kses_post button_indicator_html but line 931 writes the sanitized value into button_custom_html instead, so button_indicator_html stays raw. create_button_from_style then outputs it unescaped at lines 735-737 when button_indicator is 'html'.

When the button's configured email_recipient is 'prompt', the recipient is taken directly from the unauthenticated $_POST['recipient'] with no validation or capability check. The address is then used as the To: of wp_mail (line 1592) with the generated PDF attached, so the site's mail system can be used to send to arbitrary addresses.

Unauthenticated $_POST['cdata'] is base64-decoded and XORed with a key built only from the public _token and date index (which the page exposes in enc_data). The only check is that the result contains the token string, which is trivially satisfied, so attacker-chosen HTML is accepted as $options['text'] (line 1673) and converted via the site's API credentials.

The restriction that strips custom_javascript and on_load_javascript for non-unfiltered_html authors only runs when button_custom_html or button_indicator_html is present in the attributes (line 916). A contributor can supply custom_javascript without either attribute, and it is carried into the conversion options that are sent to the remote converter.

The URL path segment from the attacker-supplied location (same host as the permalink) is split on '/' and then rawurldecode'd at line 1082, so %2F sequences become directory separators. The result becomes the attachment name, which make_temporary_file joins onto the upload temp directory (line 1517) to create and write a file outside it when email disposition is used.

A contributor supplies button_indicator_html (and button_indicator=html) in shortcode attributes. The sanitization branch for button_indicator_html wrongly assigns wp_kses_post() output to $attrs['button_custom_html'] instead of button_indicator_html, so the raw value is stored in $options and emitted unescaped at lines 735-737 of create_button_from_style.

When the admin has set email recipient mode to 'prompt' and disposition to 'email', the unauthenticated POST parameter 'recipient' is returned as $options['email_to'] (line 1608, set at line 1718) and passed to wp_mail with the generated PDF attached (line 1592-1596), so any visitor can make the site send the PDF to an arbitrary address.

A contributor sets email_recipient_address (and email_cc, email_bcc, email_from) in shortcode attributes; these are trusted from the encrypted blob, used as $email_to (line 1560) and concatenated into the mail headers at lines 1584-1590 without validation, and wp_mail sends the server-generated PDF to that address, enabling arbitrary mail relay and header injection.

A contributor sets output_name (non-button attribute, so it goes into the encrypted options) and button_disposition=email; get_output_name() returns it unchanged (lines 1062-1063), send_email() passes it to make_temporary_file(), which concatenates it onto the upload tmp dir (line 1517) and creates the file with fopen 'x' and writes the PDF content, so ../ sequences write a new file outside the intended directory. The unauthenticated variant reaches the same sink through rawurldecode() of a URL path segment (line 1082) that can contain encoded slashes.

Contributor-authored shortcode attribute button_indicator_html (with button_indicator=html) -> eval_shortcode copies it into $options; the unfiltered_html sanitizer at 930-931 wrongly re-sanitizes button_custom_html instead of button_indicator_html, so the value is unfiltered -> create_button_from_style 736-737 echoes it raw into the page for every visitor.

Contributor-authored shortcode attribute file (also data_file, attachments, page_background, conversion_config_file, client_certificate) -> eval_shortcode stores it in encrypted custom_options -> save_as_pdf_pdfcrowd decrypts it (1636-1647) -> prepare_conv 1245-1268 places it in $files without path checks -> build_body 1107 file_get_contents() reads any server-readable path and uploads its content to api.pdfcrowd.com, with the result returned to the visitor who clicks the button.

The caller supplies args.status, which is passed through sanitize_text_field into post_status and then to wp_update_post. The only check is edit_post on the target post, so a contributor who can edit their own draft can set status to 'publish' without holding publish_posts. The publish_posts check that wp_create_post enforces is missing here.

The attacker-supplied redirect_uri query parameter in authorize_get() is sanitized but then passed to validate_redirect_uri(), which returns true for any https or localhost URI whenever the client is the static client (is_static). The authorization code is then delivered to that URI by authorize_post(). This requires a victim to approve the request, and the attacker must know the static oauth_client_id.

The rest_authentication_errors filter reads $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'] and, if it contains 'bcs-mcp/v1' anywhere (including in the query string), it returns null, which clears any WP_Error set by other plugins. This disables a site's REST lockdown for every other route, so the check is a substring match on attacker-controlled input rather than a check of the route being served.

A contributor passes edit_post on their own draft, then $args['status'] is copied without sanitization of permissions into $data['post_status'] (line 1400) and passed to wp_update_post. The publish_posts capability is never checked on this path, so a contributor can set status to 'publish' and bypass the normal review workflow.

The only check is publish_posts (held by the Author role and above, so contributors are excluded), but the tool then accepts a caller-supplied post_type (only four internal types are blocked) and post_status, and an arbitrary post_author ID (line 1385). A user with publish_posts can therefore publish pages or other post types they lack publish_pages for, and attribute posts to other users such as administrators.

wp_update_post_meta (lines 1883-1892) stores a caller-supplied string with only sanitize_text_field, so a serialized-looking string can be saved as post meta. wp_duplicate_post then calls get_post_meta on the source post and passes each value through maybe_unserialize (line 1445), which deserializes the string into a PHP object; this is exploitable only if a usable gadget chain exists on the site.

Same source as the wp_duplicate_post case: a contributor-controlled non-underscore meta string written with wp_update_post_meta is read by get_post_meta at line 2245 and passed to maybe_unserialize() at line 2248 when the page is duplicated, with the same gadget dependency.

$_REQUEST['redirect'] is passed through esc_url_raw() into $url. The only validation is strpos($url, home_url()) !== 0, a prefix match that accepts attacker hosts such as https://<site-domain>.attacker.tld. The result is then passed to wp_redirect($url). The list change at line 198 runs before this check.

Attacker-supplied name, surname, profile fields and list selections from build_subscription() are merged into an existing CONFIRMED subscriber via merge_in() and saved with save_user(), with no proof of ownership of that email address. Depends on the if_exists configuration.

Any logged-in WP user's account email is matched against subscriber emails in get_subscriber() (lines 84-86), which persists the WP-to-subscriber link and returns that subscriber. hook_newsletter_current_user then sets _trusted=true and editable=true (lines 145-146), which lets the profile-save path (profile/profile.php:106, save_profile) act on that subscriber's record without the subscriber's key. The WP email is not verified against ownership, so a registered account with a victim's address can take over that subscriber's profile. No concrete subclass ships in this tree, so this is latent and only reachable through an addon that extends NewsletterMembershipAddon.

The attacker-supplied $_REQUEST['redirect'] is passed through esc_url_raw() (line 196), and the only check is strpos($url, home_url()) !== 0 (line 200). That check is a string prefix match, so a host such as https://<site>.attacker.tld passes it, and wp_redirect() at line 207 (not wp_safe_redirect) sends the browser there. The request needs a valid subscriber key (nk), which an attacker can obtain by subscribing to the site, and an antibot check that only requires a POST with a fresh ts field.

$_REQUEST['id'] -> (int) cast -> get_email() loads any newsletter row by id with no ownership or capability check -> echo $email->message unescaped in the AJAX response; no nonce or capability check guards the handler, so drafts and private email bodies of any id are returned to any logged-in user.

$_REQUEST['id'] -> sanitize_key -> is_numeric branch -> get_email($id) loads any email row without authorization -> NewsletterComposer::regenerate($email) -> wp_send_json_success returns extract_body($email), extract_composer_options($email) and $email->subject; no nonce or capability check on the handler.

POST 'doc_type' is passed through sanitize_text_field only (line 4802), with no basename or allowlist check, and is concatenated onto the temp directory path at line 4842. A traversal value resolves to an ancestor directory, which is then walked recursively, and every .pdf, .zip or .html file found is deleted with wp_delete_file (lines 4845-4853). Access requires a valid nonce plus manage_options or manage_woocommerce.

POST 'doc_type' is sanitized only with sanitize_text_field (line 4693) and concatenated into $doc_file_loc (line 4700). A RecursiveDirectoryIterator then walks that location and adds every .pdf or .html file it finds to a zip (lines 4709-4719), so files outside the plugin temp directory can be archived. The zip is then offered for download through download_temp_zip_file.

$_POST['doc_type'] goes through sanitize_text_field(), which does not remove '../' sequences, and is then concatenated into the temp path at line 4842 (get_temp_dir('path') . '/' . $doc_type) with no realpath or allowlist check. RecursiveDirectoryIterator then walks that directory and wp_delete_file() removes every .pdf, .html or .zip file found there (line 4852). The check_write_access() gate (login, nonce, manage_options or manage_woocommerce) is the only control.

$_REQUEST['customizer_action'] is read at line 62 and used at line 63 in method_exists($this, ...) and $this->{$customizer_action}(). The $allowed_actions allowlist defined at line 61 (six methods) is never checked, so any method on the class is callable, including private and protected helpers such as delete_theme, activate_theme and save_default_template. The only gate is check_write_access() (login, nonce, manage_options or manage_woocommerce).

The POST doc_type parameter is passed through sanitize_text_field, which does not strip '/' or '..', and is concatenated onto the temp directory path at line 4842. The recursive iterator then calls wp_delete_file on every .pdf, .zip and .html file under that path, so a traversal value deletes matching files outside the temp directory.

The GET file parameter is passed through sanitize_text_field and only its extension is checked to be 'zip' (lines 4743-4745). It is then concatenated onto the temp directory (line 4747), and file_exists followed by the file read and attachment response means any existing *.zip file reachable via '../' segments is returned to the caller.

The handler checks only a WF_PKLIST_PLUGIN_NAME nonce, with no current_user_can check, then builds a payload from POST reason_id, user_email and reason_info plus server details and sends it with wp_remote_post to the vendor API. Any logged-in user holding the nonce can trigger the outbound request, so the impact is limited to unauthorized outbound submissions.

Guest checkout billing fields (get_billing_first_name/last_name/company/address_1/address_2/city/postcode, read at lines 1782-1790) are concatenated with '
' at line 1804 with no HTML escaping, then str_replace'd into the document HTML (class-customizer.php replace_placeholders) and echoed unescaped by print_it (packinglist.php:377) to a browser of an admin or the mail-link recipient. Standard WooCommerce checkout may strip tags via wc_clean, so exploitability depends on whether orders can be created without that sanitisation (needs dynamic check).
